item.title: Six arrests for smuggling migrants via Schengen airports
item.description:
Europol supported a migrant smuggling investigation involving law enforcement authorities from 17 countries. The criminal network was also engaged in document fraud and money laundering.
The action day on 22 September 2026 in Austria, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom (UK) led to six arrests, 10 house searches, and multiple seizures, including ID documents, electronic equipment, evidence, and a large amount of cash.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
item.description:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

  • Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue?

item.title: Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
item.description:
When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015, the environment looked very different.

Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon.

Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller.

Much has changed since then.

But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question:

Why are we still discussing so many of them?

Technology has advanced enormously. Investment has increased. Regulation has expanded. Cybersecurity has achieved unprecedented executive and board visibility.

Yet organisations still struggle with governance, accountability, organisational silos, short-termism and execution.

Those were management problems in 2015. They remain management problems today.

The ‘what’ was never the hardest part

One of the central observations behind my early work was that the what of cybersecurity was already reasonably well understood.

Standards, control frameworks and good practices had existed for years. Organisations could identify weaknesses, define controls and produce remediation plans. They knew what good cybersecurity looked like.

The difficult questions were always the how and the who.

How do you implement those controls across complex organisations with conflicting priorities? How do you sustain transformation over several years? Who owns the changes? Who has the authority to make them happen? And who remains accountable when progress stalls?

Those questions cannot be answered by a security framework or product. They are governance, management and leadership questions.

More than a decade later, that distinction matters even more.

Cybersecurity has progressed — but management has lagged

There is no question that cybersecurity capabilities have improved.

Detection and response have matured. Cloud security has developed rapidly. Identity management has become a central protection discipline. Security operations are increasingly automated, and AI is transforming both attack and defence.

Large organisations now operate substantial security functions supported by extensive technology portfolios, specialist providers and advisers.

But increased sophistication has not eliminated fundamental management weaknesses.

CISOs can remain accountable for issues they lack the authority to resolve. Technology and security strategies can develop on separate tracks. Business executives can still treat cybersecurity as a service delivered by the CISO rather than a dimension of the processes, applications and activities they own themselves.

Governance can produce extensive reporting without effective decision-making. Transformation programmes can identify the right problems without necessarily resolving them.

The language has evolved. The underlying management dynamics often have not.

The CISO reporting-line debate misses the point

The persistent debate around where the CISO should report illustrates the problem.

For decades, organisations have debated whether the CISO should report to the CIO, CEO, COO, CRO or another senior executive.

The CIO reporting line has attracted particular criticism because of a perceived conflict between technology delivery and cybersecurity protection.

But if decades of discussion have failed to produce a universally satisfactory answer, perhaps the real problem lies elsewhere.

Maybe the more fundamental question is: What does the organisation expect the CISO to be?

Some organisations see the CISO primarily as a technology security leader. Others position the role as an independent control function. Some expect the CISO to coordinate resilience, while others increasingly view the position as a strategic business protection role.

Those are very different jobs.

Until organisations clarify the purpose, authority and accountability of the CISO, debates about reporting lines will continue because organisational structure is being asked to compensate for ambiguity around the role itself.

Moving the CISO around the organisation chart cannot resolve that ambiguity.

CIO-CISO tension is not necessarily conflict

The supposed conflict between CIO and CISO needs a proper reality check.

The two executives inevitably face different pressures. CIOs balance cost, delivery, availability, innovation and transformation. CISOs must challenge weaknesses and ensure protection and resilience remain adequate.

That creates tension.

But tension can be constructive and does not have to become conflict.

Nor does moving the CISO outside the CIO organisation eliminate those competing priorities.

Any modern CIO should acknowledge that cybersecurity is inseparable from architecture, cloud, identity, DevOps, digital transformation, AI and resilience. CIOs and CISOs must collaborate regardless of the formal reporting structure.

What organisations really need is a governance model capable of resolving disagreements when legitimate priorities compete.

That is a leadership and management requirement, not something structural separation can solve on its own.

Cybersecurity may be undermanaged, not just underfunded

Security spending tells a similar story.

Cybersecurity investment has risen substantially over the past decade, and some organisations undoubtedly still require more resources.

But persistent weaknesses after years of increasing expenditure should lead executives to ask whether funding is always the central issue.

Money can buy technology, people and expertise. It can finance transformation and accelerate remediation.

What it cannot automatically do is establish strategic priorities, create clear accountability, resolve organisational politics, force collaboration or ensure transformation programmes achieve their objectives.

Again, those outcomes depend on leadership and management.

Cybersecurity can be underfunded, but quite often it is also undermanaged.

The distinction matters because it changes the executive conversation from “How much more do we need to spend?” to “Are we converting the investment we already make into sustainable capability?”

Compliance is necessary, but it cannot substitute for management

The expansion of regulation and certification schemes has created genuine benefits. It can establish minimum standards, impose accountability and force cybersecurity onto executive agendas.

But compliance has inherent limitations.

An organisation can satisfy formal requirements while carrying substantial structural weaknesses. An audit finding can be closed without addressing the management problem behind it. Certification can demonstrate that processes exist without proving that an organisation will behave effectively during a serious incident.

When showing activity becomes more important than building sustainable capabilities, compliance runs the risk of providing reassurance without necessarily delivering protection.

Board awareness was only the first step

Over the past decade, cybersecurity has also achieved something the industry demanded for years: It has reached the boardroom.

That matters, but board visibility does not automatically produce effective governance.

Many organizations are totally technology-dependent and their boards already understand the importance of cyber protection and resilience

The old argument that CISOs need to convince boards of the importance of cybersecurity and the need to invest in it, is increasingly outdated.

The more important issue is what boards do next.

Boards should challenge whether strategic priorities are clear, whether executive accountability is effective, whether transformation is progressing and whether investment is creating sustainable capability.

They also need to understand whether assumptions about resilience have been tested.

Board awareness was necessary. Board responsibility is the more important issue now.

Breaking the cybersecurity spiral of failure

These management weaknesses help explain why cybersecurity transformation repeatedly loses momentum.

A serious incident creates urgency. Urgency releases funding. Remediation accelerates and visible progress is made.

Eventually, the pressure declines. Executive attention moves elsewhere. Longer-term structural problems become harder to prioritise. Transformation slows down. Then another incident restarts the process.

I have described this as the Cybersecurity Spiral of Failure.

Organisations can spend substantial amounts during every cycle and make genuine technical improvements while leaving intact the management conditions that created the weaknesses in the first place.

Poor accountability remains. Governance struggles with difficult decisions. Priorities change. Corporate or geographical silos inhibit execution. Short-term pressures displace long-term transformation.

Breaking that cycle requires management discipline and strategic continuity — not simply another security programme.

Cybersecurity cannot remain the CISO’s problem

Perhaps the most important lesson is that cybersecurity cannot become sustainable while organisations continue treating it primarily as the CISO’s responsibility.

The CISO has an essential role in providing expertise, strategic direction, coordination and challenge.

But the organisation must execute.

The CIO needs to ensure technology architectures and services are secure and resilient. Business executives need to accept accountability for the processes and applications they own. Corporate functions must discharge the security responsibilities attached to their authority. Executive management must resolve competing priorities. The board must provide oversight and strategic continuity.

The CISO cannot substitute for those responsibilities.

The principle should be straightforward: Accountability must follow authority.

The objective is not to turn every executive into a cybersecurity specialist. It is to make cybersecurity part of normal management.

The technology will change. The management principles won’t

There will always be another technology wave.

AI will continue to transform business practices. Quantum computing may force major cryptographic transformation. Cloud architectures will continue evolving. Digital ecosystems will become even more interconnected.

The security industry will respond with new products, frameworks and methodologies.

But organisations need management principles capable of surviving those technology cycles: Clear priorities. Accountability aligned with authority. Governance capable of turning disagreement into decisions. Strong CIO-CISO collaboration. Genuine business ownership. Sustained board oversight. And disciplined execution.

That brings us back to the question we started with: Why do cybersecurity observations from 2015 still sound so contemporary?

Because many of the hardest cybersecurity problems were never primarily technological.

They concern leadership, accountability, governance, organisational politics, short-termism and execution. They cannot be patched, outsourced or solved simply by moving the CISO to another reporting line.

They have to be managed.

Cybersecurity has become a core business protection capability. It is fundamentally a management challenge supported by technology — not a technology challenge that management somehow needs to accommodate.

item.title: How Claude Code’s 256KB blind spot put developers’ secrets in the preview pane
item.description:
Simply asking Anthropic’s Claude Code to review an HTML file could hand attackers access to a developer’s machine, cloud credentials and software development environment, according to a new Noma Security finding.

Noma’s researchers found a vulnerability affecting Anthropic’s Claude Code Desktop app that could allow malicious JavaScript embedded in an HTML file to execute without further user interaction, potentially exposing sensitive host files. The flaw, called SneakPeek, specifically affected the application’s automated preview pane, which renders HTML files generated or modified by Claude.

“This is a strong example of how emerging technologies are reshaping the attack surface,” said Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck. “Attackers are increasingly targeting the AI ecosystem, exploiting implicit trust relationships between models, agents, tools, data sources, and connected services.”

An attacker could exploit the bug by planting a malicious file in a public repository and waiting for a developer to ask Claude Code to inspect it, Noma said in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Wednesday.

Once the application rendered the file, the script could read local files and exfiltrate sensitive data, including AWS credentials, GitHub secrets and SSH private keys, to a remote server.

The flaw has been assigned a high-severity CVSS score of 8.7, while a CVE ID is not yet available. Noma says Anthropic collaborated with Noma Labs during the disclosure process and fully resolved the issue.

“Anthropic confirmed they are preparing a GitHub Security Advisory and have requested a CVE for it,” Eli Ainhorn, senior AI vulnerability researcher at Noma, told CSO. “We expect it to be available soon. The CVSS score is 8.7 High (v4.0), assigned by Anthropic.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

A 256KB threshold allowed local files to leak

Noma traced SneakPeek to three architectural gaps in Claude Code Desktop’s preview mechanism, which uses an Electron-based Chromium rendering panel to display HTML content.

The first involved a file-size threshold that changed how the application handled HTML documents. Files smaller than 256KB were converted into base64-encoded data: URLs with a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) that blocked script execution. Files exceeding that threshold were instead written to disk and loaded directly as “file://” URLs, bypassing the CSP protections applied to smaller files.

The second problem was the origin assigned to the rendered content. Loading the larger files through file:// gave the preview renderer access to the local filesystem in Chromium rather than confining it to an isolated, opaque origin, the researchers said.

The third weakness was an inactive request filter. Although the application has a mechanism intended to block file: // access, Noma found that the filter was not active during static file rendering, including when developers reviewed local code test reports.

“Relying on size-based thresholds or client-side filters for security boundaries is inherently fragile,” Lewis said. “Development machines hold high-value operational secrets—SSH private keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configurations, and OAuth session tokens.”

Compromising a developer’s local workstation is effectively a direct route into corporate cloud infrastructure, he warned.

Noma found that Anthropic’s initial patch could be bypassed. “The initial patch blocked the preview pane from making direct file read requests from the main page context, but we found that by moving the file-reading code into a Web Worker, a background thread that browsers run separately from the main page, the requests originated from a context the patch didn’t cover,” Ainhorn explained.

The researchers reported the bypass, prompting a deeper architectural fix before the vulnerability was fully resolved.

Risk beyond the AI model

The malicious script ran inside the preview pane’s rendering process, rather than as an action performed by the AI agent itself. That defeats the assumption that security controls meant for the model are protecting all AI workflows.

“The protections were real, they just didn’t cover every path,” Ainhorn said. “Organizations need to keep AI coding tools updated, stop leaving long-lived credentials on developer machines, and use scoped, short-lived tokens where possible. That alone would have limited what this exploit could grab.”

According to Sysdig’s senior cybersecurity strategist Crystal Morin, agent-level logs would not necessarily capture the execution. File reads and outbound network connections would instead be visible at the runtime layer, where defenders need appropriate monitoring, Morin said. “The endpoint is where AI agents start, but their blast radius extends to the cloud,“ she added, warning that routine work with AI tools can expose credentials with consequences far beyond the workstation.

item.title: As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
item.description:
Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages.

Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS).

The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials.

Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities.

“Working together, and with the assistance of AI tools, we connected accounts, websites, and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them,” Steven Masada, associate general counsel and GM for Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post. “What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.”

The evolving PhaaS marketplace

Collectively, YAM Store and the kits and tools sold within it enabled the sending of more than 1 billion messages to 75,000-plus organizations worldwide. More than 750 million of those were sent to Microsoft customers alone, and ultimately generated “tens of millions of dollars” for criminal operators. 

Investigation into the marketplace began in late 2025 after Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) notified Microsoft of “a wave of fraud and scam activity” targeting people and businesses in Japan. Researchers expected to find multiple individual campaigns; instead, they discovered a “sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace.” The probe expanded globally and involved the efforts of several other law enforcement agencies, as well as companies like Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs.

The YAM Store served as an initial access broker (IAB), operating much like an online marketplace; in this case, the merchandise was fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts and other ready-made tools used to carry out scams like credential and data theft. Customers could browse, compare prices, and make purchases. Available tools were arranged based on age and subscription and environment types (like .edu or .org sites).

In some cases, criminal operators were able to register internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire, then rebuilt them to appear active. They targeted specific sectors (like non-profits or education) to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts to later sell through the YAM store.

The researchers discovered that the YAM Store evolved as different kits became available, and identified three popular PhaaS kits: Iron Man System, CoGUI, and Haozi.

The newer Iron Man system came to the fore in mid-2026. It provided pre-built lure pages capturing any victim-submitted data. The lure sites impersonated healthcare providers, police departments, government agencies, postal and courier services, toll and transportation authorities, tax agencies, banks, telecoms, and retailers. Through test purchases and intelligence work, investigators discovered more than 2,300 templates impersonating organizations across more than 150 countries.

Iron Man effectively expanded the PhaaS model by giving criminals access to thousands of ready-made templates tailored to specific industries, languages, and regions. Masada noted that many “used the appearance of official authority to pressure victims into making payments or disclosing sensitive personal information. Instead of creating fraudulent websites themselves, criminals could quickly deploy pages designed to steal passwords, payment information, and other personal data.”

The kits were also equipped with advanced evasion techniques such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations.

Masada emphasized that, while an organization or government entity may have been presented among the template offerings, it does not indicate that its systems were compromised.

However, members of the Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit wrote in a blog post, “the scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses.”

The importance of cyber hygiene

In nearly all observed cases, phishing lures presented “prescriptive scam red flags,” Microsoft researchers explained: Urgency and time-sensitive tasks.

They advised that users have a basic understanding of common phishing techniques and should be educated to always verify with the purported sender before clicking a link supposedly taking them to a login page, even when the task involves signing in to a known, secure account.

Beyond this, they said, sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. In Microsoft Azure interactions since 2021, for example, users are prompted to “cancel” or “continue” at login, but this is often missing from phishing sign-ins, the researchers noted.

Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks; the researchers suggested an initial step of passwordless tools like passkeys and multifactor authentication (MFA) across organizations.

“Invoke the principles of least privilege and zero trust to significantly slow down threat actors who might have been able to gain initial access and buy time for defenders to respond,” the researchers noted. These steps can help lock down global administrator roles in particular.

They also advised additional actions including the use of the Microsoft Authenticator app for passkeys and MFA; configuration of the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policy to apply to internal recipients; complementing MFA with conditional access policies; and only allowing MFA and passkey registrations from trusted locations and devices.

item.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
item.description: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

item.title: Ransomware extortion gets personal as attackers target employees’ families
item.description:
Ransomware attackers are expanding their tactics beyond encrypting corporate systems and threatening to leak stolen data. They are increasingly using AI in attacks, exploiting organizations’ own AI systems and even using physical intimidation by threatening employees and their families to pressure companies into paying ransoms.

The Semperis’ 2026 Ransomware Risk Report found that 84% of surveyed ransomware victims experienced attacks involving AI, while 87% reported attacks targeting identity infrastructure. It also highlighted that attackers are exploiting technology and extending pressure beyond corporate networks to the people connected to their targets.

While 41% of respondents reported physical or psychological intimidation, 37% said employees’ friends or family members had been threatened. The survey in the first half of 2026 covered 1,200 IT and security professionals across nine countries, spanning eight sectors including finance, healthcare, manufacturing, critical infrastructure and government.

Extortion is moving beyond corporate networks

Ransomware initially relied on encrypting files and demanding payment for a decryption key. As organizations improve their ability to recover from ransomware attacks using backups and recovery systems, attackers increasingly adopt double extortion, combining encryption with data theft and threats to expose or sell stolen information.

Now, they are adding personal intimidation to their tactics. These include threatening texts, letters or packages, threats against family members and friends, physical intrusion, abduction, bodily harm and stalking. 

The report found that 25% of respondents said employees or family members had been doxed (their identities were revealed online without their consent), while 23% reported swatting, where they were harassed by fabricated emergency reports resulted in law enforcement being dispatched to a victim’s location. About 25% reported that employees or their family members required medical or psychological treatment, while 24% said they had hired additional security. And around 14% were even forced to change jobs, office locations, or move to a new home.

“Threats that target corporate employees beyond corporate borders are an unusual new phenomenon that distracts employees from being laser-focused while at work on the job at hand. Now you’re trying to figure out how to protect yourself and loved ones against a threat that has crossed the boundary from work to personal life,” Chris Inglis, former US national cyber director and Semperis Strategic Advisor, noted in the report.

Despite the fact that an organization might agree to suffer financial losses and restore their servers while rejecting ransom, the threat to hurt one of their employees’ spouse or kid creates additional pressure to decision making due to the fact that it involves more people than just a business.

“Attackers do this by trying to build up a picture of an employee’s personal life using the information that is already available or leaked somewhere else before. It can include public information posted on social media accounts, professional networks, data broker databases, previously leaked information, and even information available in the attacked company’s network. Artificial intelligence can help speed up the process of correlating this information and thus create a personalized threat for a person,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and CEO at Primus Partners.

Exploiting enterprise AI

As enterprises connect AI agents to corporate data, applications, and identity systems, these tools are becoming another potential attack surface. Semperis found that 44% of respondents experienced attacks involving the manipulation of their own AI agents or systems.

Courtney Guss, Semperis AVP of Crisis Management, said that if a company is adopting AI agents, one should consider that at some point, those agents will try to compromise identity systems, even if that action isn’t meant to be malicious. She added, “AI agents typically try to accomplish their assigned tasks by any means they can. One way they can gain more ability to operate in the environment is by getting permissions to other systems. The fastest path to get those permissions is to compromise your identity system, which effectively puts the agent into ‘god mode,’ enabling it to grant itself whichever permissions it needs to accomplish its task. Unfortunately, the agent then becomes a ticking time bomb.”

Dhar noted that AI can be used by attackers to speed up the processes of reconnaissance, personalize social engineering, and accelerate the processing of information. Besides, weakly secured AI agents are another entry point for hackers into systems. In most cases, AI serves as an accelerating tool but does not stand alone behind attacks. While organizations increase their capabilities for restoring encrypted data, attackers continue to become even more aggressive in exploiting weaknesses of people and organizations.

Closing the security gaps

The evolving threat landscape raises questions about whether existing security controls and incident response plans are equipped to handle attacks that exploit AI systems and extend to employees’ personal lives. Experts suggest CSOs should take care of identity security, test recovery and limited access to AI systems. They should ensure robust, phishing-proof two-factor authentication of privileged accounts, least privilege approach, safe backups of identity systems and testing restoration.

“AI agents used by the organization should have clearly defined owners and limited permissions. They should have human approval for all high-priority actions. The organization should also minimize information retention and access to sensitive personal information of employees,” added Dhar.

In case an employee’s family is attacked, they should have a confidential channel to report intimidation, while HR, legal, cybersecurity, and corporate security teams should know when and how to escalate cases to law enforcement. Even tabletop exercises should simulate scenarios involving compromised identity systems, threatened data leaks, and threats against employees’ families.

item.title: Attackers exploit Palo Alto PAN-OS flaw for root access as CISA orders three-day fix
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting a newly disclosed flaw in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software to run code with root privileges, and US federal agencies have been ordered to fix it and check for compromise by October 17.

Palo Alto Networks disclosed the vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, in a security advisory published October 14. The flaw “enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall,” the advisory said.

“Very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface,” the company said. It rated the flaw 8.6 on the CVSS 4.0 scale, which is high severity, and assigned it its highest urgency rating. The company classified it as CWE-94, a code injection weakness.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-0322 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, citing evidence of active exploitation.

Forensic triage required

The catalog entry marks the flaw as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. The directive “establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied,” CISA said in its alert announcing the addition.

The entry directs agencies to apply the vendor’s mitigations or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. It lists the flaw’s use in ransomware campaigns as unknown.

Yih Khai Wong, senior research manager for security services at IDC Asia/Pacific, said security teams should trace who can reach the management interface from outside a trusted network and review admin login history for unusual activity. “They should also check firewall configurations for unexpected changes, since a compromised device can be quietly reconfigured to remain compromised,” he said.

“Patching is only part of the response,” said Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer. He said teams should check Panorama and every managed firewall and preserve evidence before making changes.

Affected products and fixes

The vulnerability affects PAN-OS on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama, in both virtual and M-Series form, according to the advisory. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected.

“No special configuration is required to be affected by this issue,” the advisory said.

Palo Alto Networks has released fixed versions for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2, with hotfix releases listed for each maintenance line. The advisory gave an estimated release date of Oct. 15 for PAN-OS 11.2.16, the upgrade path for customers on 11.2.14 and 11.2.15. Customers on unsupported versions should move to a supported fixed release, the company advisory said.

Wong said management access to any device still awaiting a fix should be locked down, or compensating controls should be applied on the device.

How attackers get in

The advisory does not say how attackers obtained that access, when exploitation began, or how many customers were affected.

“The entry point probably isn’t the bug itself, but weak management-access hygiene,” Wong said. He cited admin credentials stolen through phishing or reuse, management interfaces left reachable from the internet, or an earlier compromise that gave an attacker valid logins.

“Once they can execute code as root on a firewall, they have control over a device that enforces security across the network,” Dubey said.

Palo Alto Networks said the flaw was discovered internally.

No workarounds yet

“No known workarounds exist for this issue,” the advisory said.

Customers with a Threat Prevention subscription can enable Threat IDs 510046 and 510047, which the company said provide limited coverage and require SSL decryption. “Variations may exist that cannot currently be detected,” the advisory’s FAQ said.

The company said risk “is highest when you allow access to the management interface from external IP addresses on the internet” and recommended restricting access to trusted internal IP addresses.

Wong said the narrow gap is a warning because a jump box only limits or slows access and does not reduce the damage from an intruder holding valid credentials. “The real risks are credential security and detecting misuse after login, not simply restricting the front door,” he said.

Wong said enterprises should ask vendors why management interfaces keep emerging as the weak point instead of being locked down by default, how they detect misuse of valid admin credentials, and how quickly patches reach every supported version. “Until every affected release is covered, production systems remain exposed,” he said.

“If an attacker gains control of a firewall, organizations need a clear way to determine whether the device can still be trusted,” Dubey said. Palo Alto Networks did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Cisco warns of actively exploited Secure Email Gateway flaw
item.description:
A critical vulnerability affecting Cisco’s Secure Email Gateway product is allowing attackers to
write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. In an advisory issued on Wednesday, the company urged customers to apply available fixes after confirming that the flaw is being exploited in the wild.

The flaw affects the product’s Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature and stems from improper handling of email attachments when the File Reputation service is enabled. By sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment through a vulnerable appliance, an attacker can execute commands with root privileges.

Cisco released software updates to address the flaw, but warns that there are no workarounds that address the vulnerability.

Exploitation is subject to preconditions

Tracked as CVE-2026-76519, the vulnerability affects physical and virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances running vulnerable Cisco AsyncOS software, provided two conditions are met. The File Reputation service needs to be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version is earlier than 25.3.0.5525.

The File Reputation service is part of Cisco AMP, which helps assess the reputation of files passing through the email gateway. In this case, improper handling of attachments creates an opportunity for an attacker to write arbitrary files to the underlying operating system. Successful exploitation can then lead to root-level command execution, potentially enabling further compromise of the appliance.

Cisco warns that attackers who compromise an appliance could access private SSH keys used to authenticate between members of an appliance cluster, potentially allowing them to compromise other cluster members. Attackers with root access may also remove or conceal evidence of their activity.

Cisco recommends checking the appliance’s system logs for indicators of compromise using the command grep “System Security” system_logs. However, a clean result should not replace broader investigation: the vendor advises administrators to cross-check external network and firewall logs for suspicious traffic, including unexpected uploads from affected appliances or downloads from malicious IP addresses.

Patches are available, but incident response matters

Cisco lists AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 as fixed releases for the corresponding software branches. Customers on AsyncOS 16.0 are advised to migrate to a fixed release. The vendor also said the fix is available through Content Scanner Tools version 25.3.0.5525 and later, and that updating the tools does not require a software upgrade or appliance restart.

For potentially compromised virtual appliances, Cisco recommends preserving forensic evidence before rebuilding the system, deploying a clean virtual machine, rebuilding its configuration without importing previous configuration files, and renewing credentials and cryptographic materials.

Organizations should also assess other appliances in the same cluster. The company said it has already deployed the fixed Content Scanner Tools package for its Secure Email Cloud Gateway environment. The advisory does not disclose the number of victims or identify the attackers behind the exploitation.
